title: CAN CHRISTIANS HAVE ANXIETY? YES—AND WHAT JESUS SAYS NEXT MAY CHANGE THE WAY YOU SEE YOURSELF
paragraphs: CAN CHRISTIANS HAVE ANXIETY? YES—AND WHAT JESUS SAYS NEXT MAY CHANGE THE WAY YOU SEE YOURSELF

You can love Jesus deeply and still feel your chest tighten at 2:17 in the morning. Anxiety does not automatically mean your faith is fake. But Jesus loves you too much to leave fear sitting on the throne of your heart.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that happens when everyone thinks you are strong.
You know how to smile at church.
You know when to say, “God is good.”
You know the verses.
You know the worship songs.
You know how to encourage somebody else when their world is collapsing.
And yet there are nights when you lie in bed staring into the darkness while your mind rehearses disasters that have not happened.
What if I lose my job?
What if the test result is bad?
What if my marriage never heals?
What if my child walks away from God?
What if I cannot pay this?
What if they leave?
What if I fail?
What if tomorrow destroys everything I am trying to hold together today?
Your body is exhausted, but your mind refuses to sleep.
Your heart beats harder.
You pray.
You try to surrender it.
Five minutes later, you are carrying it again.
Then something even heavier enters the room.
Shame.
Because now you are not merely anxious.
You are anxious about being anxious.

You remember Jesus telling His disciples not to worry. You remember Paul saying not to be anxious about anything. And suddenly the frightened believer begins conducting a spiritual trial against himself.
“If I really trusted God, would I feel this way?”
“If my faith were stronger, would I still be struggling?”
“Is God disappointed in me?”
“Can a real Christian even have anxiety?”
Please stay with me.
Because the answer matters.
And before this is over, we need to confront not only what anxiety whispers about tomorrow, but what shame has been whispering about your relationship with God.
Yes.
Christians can experience anxiety.
Deeply committed Christians can experience anxiety.

People who genuinely love Jesus can experience fear, distress, overwhelming circumstances, sleepless nights, physical symptoms, and seasons when their thoughts feel frighteningly difficult to control.
But Scripture does not therefore tell us that anxiety should become our master, identity, theology, or permanent residence.
There is a difference between experiencing anxiety and enthroning anxiety.
There is a difference between being attacked by fear and surrendering your life to fear.
There is a difference between a frightened nervous system and a faithless heart.
And there is a difference between Jesus correcting our anxious thinking and Jesus condemning an anxious person.
That distinction changes everything.
When Jesus speaks about worry in Matthew 6, the Greek text says:
“μὴ μεριμνᾶτε τῇ ψυχῇ ὑμῶν…”
Mē merimnate tē psychē hymōn…
“Do not be anxious/worried about your life…”
The key word is related to μεριμνάω — merimnaō, a verb used for being anxious, concerned, or occupied with care.
Jesus is speaking about the consuming worry surrounding ordinary human needs—food, drink, clothing, tomorrow.
But notice what Jesus does next.
He does not humiliate frightened people.
He redirects their vision.
He tells them to look at birds.
Imagine that.

The Son of God is addressing people living in a world without modern insurance systems, refrigerators, retirement accounts, instant banking, modern medicine, or guaranteed salaries—and He points toward the sky.
Look.
The birds do not control tomorrow.
Yet your heavenly Father feeds them.
Then comes the question that anxiety desperately needs to hear:
Are you not worth much more than they are?
Jesus moves the discussion from circumstances to Fatherhood.
That is crucial.
Because anxiety says, “Everything depends on you.”
Jesus says, “You have a Father.”
Anxiety says, “Predict everything.”
Jesus says, “Look at your Father.”
Anxiety says, “Control tomorrow.”
Jesus says, “Seek first the kingdom of God.”
Anxiety says, “What if?”
Jesus keeps bringing us back to “Who?”
Who feeds the birds?
Who clothes the grass?
Who knows what you need?
Who holds tomorrow?
Who calls you His own?
The biblical answer to anxiety is not pretending frightening circumstances do not exist.
It is learning that frightening circumstances do not have the final word.
And perhaps that is why your anxiety has been so exhausting.
You have been trying to carry a tomorrow that God never gave you permission to carry today.
You keep mentally traveling into a future where God has not abandoned you—but in your imagination, you arrive there without Him.
Read that again.
Anxiety often imagines tomorrow’s trouble while forgetting tomorrow’s grace.
You imagine the diagnosis.
But not the grace.
You imagine the rejection.
But not the grace.
You imagine losing the job.
But not the grace.
You imagine the funeral.
But not the grace.
You imagine everything falling apart.
But somehow, in the terrifying movie playing inside your head, the God who sustained you through everything before this mysteriously disappears from the next scene.
Jesus brings the Father back into the picture.
And that does not mean painful things cannot happen.
Christianity never promises that.
Jesus never promised His followers an untouched life.
The cross itself destroys any version of Christianity that says faithful people never suffer.
Our Savior was called “a man of sorrows” in Isaiah 53:3.
In Gethsemane, Jesus experienced profound anguish as the cross approached.
He was not sinful.
He was not faithless.
He was not spiritually defective.
He was the spotless Son of God.
That alone should make us extraordinarily careful before looking at a suffering believer and saying, “If you had enough faith, you would not feel distress.”
That sentence can wound people Scripture was meant to shepherd.
There are Christians who have been afraid to admit what they are experiencing because they think honesty will expose them as spiritual failures.
So they hide.
They smile.
They serve.
They post Bible verses.
They worship with everyone else.
Then they go home and unravel privately.
Somewhere along the way they began believing that Christianity required them to pretend.
But Christianity begins with the opposite.
Confession.
Truth.
Coming into the light.
God does not need your performance.
He already knows.
He knows about the racing thoughts.
He knows about the tears you wiped away before anyone walked into the room.
He knows why that particular phone call frightens you.
He knows why money makes your stomach tighten.
He knows what happened in your childhood.
He knows what you lost.
He knows the memory that keeps returning.
He knows what you are afraid will happen again.
And Scripture does not tell you to hide that burden from Him.
It tells you where to put it.
Peter writes:
Notice the tenderness underneath the command.
Why cast it?
Not because God is irritated that you have it.
Because He cares for you.
The invitation rests upon the character of God.
Your anxiety is not too embarrassing for Him.
Your questions are not too messy.
Your trembling does not frighten Him.
Your tears do not inconvenience Him.
Bring it.
Bring the thought you are ashamed to admit.
Bring the fear you have repeated a thousand times.
Bring the uncertainty.
Bring the future.
Bring the person you cannot control.
Bring the situation you cannot fix.
Bring the medical appointment.
Bring the overdue bill.
Bring the marriage.
Bring the child.
Bring the grief.
Bring tomorrow.
Not because prayer is a magical technique that guarantees every anxious sensation disappears immediately.
But because you were never created to be your own god.
That is where Philippians 4 becomes breathtakingly practical.
Paul writes:
Mēden merimnate…
“Be anxious about nothing…”
But stopping there can make the verse sound like Paul merely shouted, “STOP WORRYING.”
He did not.
The sentence continues:
“…ἀλλ’ ἐν παντὶ τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ τῇ δεήσει…”
“…but in everything, by prayer and supplication…”
And then:
“…μετ’ εὐχαριστίας…”
“…with thanksgiving…”
Paul does not merely identify what must leave.
He tells us what must replace it.
Prayer.
Supplication.
Thanksgiving.
Requests brought before God.
Then comes the promise of Philippians 4:7—not that every circumstance instantly changes, but that the peace of God guards the believer’s heart and mind in Christ Jesus.
Do you see the movement?
Anxiety turns inward.
Prayer turns upward.
Anxiety rehearses possibilities.
Prayer presents realities to God.
Anxiety says, “I must solve everything.”
Prayer says, “Father, I cannot carry this without You.”
Thanksgiving then remembers what panic forgets.
God has been faithful before.
This does not mean you should feel guilty every time anxiety returns.
Sometimes surrender happens again five minutes later.
Then surrender again.
And again.
And again.
You may have to place the same fear into God’s hands fifty times before lunch.
That does not necessarily mean the first prayer was fake.
It means you are learning dependence.
A toddler learning to walk falls repeatedly.
A disciple learning trust may repeatedly discover how quickly the heart reaches back for what it surrendered.
Bring it back.
Again.
There is no prize for pretending you are stronger than you are.
The Gospel is not the announcement that strong people finally learned how to rescue themselves.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who could not rescue themselves were rescued by Jesus Christ.
This is where anxiety becomes part of a much larger story.
Because your deepest problem is not anxiety.
Mine is not either.
Our deepest problem is sin and separation from a holy God.
And no breathing technique, productivity system, financial security, relationship, medication, vacation, motivational speech, or perfectly controlled future can reconcile sinful humanity to God.
We needed a Savior.
Jesus came.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He bore sin upon the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Christ receives something infinitely greater than a promise that nothing frightening will ever happen.
We receive God Himself.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Adoption.
Eternal life.
A living hope.
And suddenly the greatest “what if” of the human soul has an answer.
“What if I die?”
For the person who belongs to Jesus, death itself has lost its ultimate claim.
Christ is risen.
That does not make grief painless.
It makes grief temporary.
It does not make suffering imaginary.
It makes suffering unable to write the final chapter.
It does not mean Christians never tremble.
It means trembling Christians can still cling to an unshakable Christ.
Maybe you needed those words.
Because perhaps you have secretly believed Jesus is standing on the other side of your anxiety with folded arms, disappointed that you have not fixed yourself yet.
Look again at the Gospel.
Those are not folded arms.
Those are pierced hands.
The hands of Christ tell a completely different story.
“I already knew how broken you were when I came for you.”
Jesus did not discover your weakness after saving you.
He knew.
He knew every night you would struggle.
Every relapse into worry.
Every frightened prayer.
Every question.
Every moment you would need mercy again.
And He went to the cross knowing your entire story.
This is grace.
Not permission to make peace with unbelief.
Not permission to let fear rule unquestioned.
Grace gives us somewhere to run while Christ transforms us.
And sometimes that transformation includes accepting help.
Please hear this carefully.
Seeking appropriate professional help for persistent or debilitating anxiety is not automatically evidence of weak faith.
Christians pray when sick, and Christians may also see physicians.
Christians trust God for provision, and Christians still work.
Christians ask God for wisdom, and Christians still seek wise counsel.
Ordinary means of care and dependence upon God are not enemies.

If anxiety is severe, persistent, producing significant impairment, or making daily life difficult, seeking qualified medical or mental-health care can be an act of wisdom rather than spiritual surrender.
And if someone has taught you that every anxiety symptom proves there must be some secret sin you have not confessed, Scripture requires more careful handling than that.

Sometimes anxiety can indeed be intensified by sinful patterns—trying to control everything, refusing to trust God, obsession with possessions, fear of people, or carrying responsibilities God never assigned us.
Those things should be confronted honestly.
Repentance matters.
But suffering is not always a simple equation where symptom equals personal sin.
Read Job.
Look at the Psalms.
Watch Elijah collapse exhausted under the broom tree in 1 Kings 19.
Listen to David pour anguish onto the page.
The Bible is remarkably unembarrassed by distressed human beings.
Maybe modern Christians should be less embarrassed too.
Because somewhere reading this right now is a believer who has been fighting silently.
You have wondered whether anybody would understand.
You have wondered whether admitting it would make people question your Christianity.
Maybe this is the moment the hiding stops.
You do not need to explain everything publicly.
Those three words are enough.
Pray.
We were never meant to suffer as isolated usernames.
We are the body of Christ.
Maybe someone else needs to know they are not the only Christian who has cried while praying.
Not the only Christian who has worshiped while afraid.
Not the only Christian who believes God is sovereign and still sometimes struggles to quiet their mind.
Faith and emotional struggle can exist in the same human heart.
The question is not merely whether fear knocks on the door.
The question is who gets the house.
Jesus is Lord.
Not anxiety.
Jesus is Lord.
Not your diagnosis.
Jesus is Lord.
Not tomorrow.
Jesus is Lord.
Not your bank account.
Jesus is Lord.
Not that person’s opinion.
Jesus is Lord.
Not the worst thing your imagination can manufacture tonight.
And perhaps Christian courage is not always feeling fearless.
Sometimes courage looks like whispering, “Jesus, I trust You,” with shaking hands.
Sometimes victory is not a dramatic emotional breakthrough.
Sometimes victory is refusing to run from Christ while you are hurting.
Sometimes faith looks like making the appointment.
Taking the next responsible step.
Opening your Bible.
Calling someone trustworthy.
Getting out of bed.
Praying one sentence because that is all you can manage.
“Jesus, help me.”
Peter once sank beneath the waves after fear overwhelmed him.
His prayer was hardly sophisticated:
“Lord, save me!”
And Jesus reached for him.
Perhaps you have spent years believing you need an impressive prayer.
Maybe tonight you simply need an honest one.
“Lord, save me.”
“Lord, help me.”
“Father, I am afraid.”
“Jesus, I cannot carry tomorrow anymore.”
“Heavenly Father, teach me to trust You today.”
That is not glamorous Christianity.
It is dependent Christianity.
And dependence is where grace becomes beautiful.
You are seen.
You are loved.
And there is still hope in Jesus.
Not because you need another piece of content sitting forgotten in a folder, but because there may come another night when fear begins preaching to you again.
When it does, return to what is true.
Your feelings are real.
They are not sovereign.
Your circumstances matter.
They are not Lord.
Tomorrow exists.
But tomorrow belongs to God.
Your anxiety may be loud.
Jesus is greater.
Not as proof of your spirituality. Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
Somebody may never tell you.
Somebody may read the first paragraph at midnight and finally realize that struggling with anxiety does not automatically mean Jesus has abandoned them.
If one frightened person encounters the truth of Christ because you were willing to put this message where they could see it, that share mattered.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can also be one practical way—among many—to steward what God has entrusted to you for the encouragement of others. Grace cannot be bought.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has drifted.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person asking questions about Christianity.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
But never confuse resources with the Source.
The goal is not Gospel Warrior.
The goal is Jesus.
The goal is not merely becoming calmer.
The goal is becoming more like Christ.
The goal is not constructing a life where nothing can hurt you.
The goal is knowing the One who will never leave you when life hurts.
So…
Can Christians have anxiety?
Yes.
But anxiety does not get to rename you.
You are not “the anxious one” before you are Christ’s.
You are not your worst night.
You are not your racing thoughts.
You are not the frightening possibility your mind keeps rehearsing.
If you are in Christ, your story is being written by Someone who walked out of a grave.
And that means fear does not get the final sentence.
Maybe tonight your circumstances will not immediately change.
Maybe the bill is still there.
The diagnosis is still uncertain.
The relationship is still complicated.
The grief still hurts.
The unanswered question is still unanswered.
But something can change before tomorrow arrives.
You can stop demanding that your frightened heart become omniscient.
You can stop requiring yourself to know how everything ends.
You can open trembling hands.
You can give tomorrow back to its rightful Owner.
And you can whisper:
“Jesus, I do not know what happens next.
But You do.
I do not understand everything.
But You are still good.
I cannot control tomorrow.
But tomorrow belongs to You.
Forgive my unbelief.
Teach me to trust You.
Hold me when I cannot hold myself.
And whatever comes…
do not let fear have what belongs to You.”
Your heart.
Your worship.
Your future.
Your life.
Give it to Christ.
Again tonight.
Again tomorrow.
Again whenever fear returns.
Because the Christian story was never about frightened people becoming powerful enough to save themselves.
It is about helpless sinners discovering that the Savior who died for them is strong enough to carry them home.
So when anxiety whispers, “What if everything falls apart?”
Remember the empty tomb.
Everything that looked finished on Friday was being rewritten by Sunday.
Your fear may be writing tonight’s sentence—but Jesus still holds the pen.
Jesus Christ is still calling frightened people out of hiding.
Still forgiving sinners.
Still restoring the broken.
Still carrying burdens.
Still turning repentance into restoration.
Still turning shame into testimony.
Still turning graves into beginnings.
Still rewriting stories the world thought were already over.
And perhaps the chapter you are most afraid of is the very chapter where you will discover just how faithfully Christ has been holding you.
